# True or false: Ways of working

Story points, velocity, sprints and estimates: some of the most repeated beliefs in software are not in the Scrum Guide at all. Find out which ones.

10 statements (Foundation 5, Standard 5). Decide whether each one is true or false before you open the answer. Every answer says why and links to the page that teaches it.

Prefer the terminal? From the repository root, run `python3 exercises/quiz.py --area ways-of-working`.

### 1. Story points and velocity are required parts of Scrum.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** The Scrum Guide (2020 edition) does not mention story points or velocity. They are an optional technique that many teams add. You can run Scrum fully and forecast from throughput instead.

Read more: [playbook/ways-of-working/agile-and-scrum.md](../../playbook/ways-of-working/agile-and-scrum.md)

</details>

### 2. Comparing velocity between teams is a fair way to see which team is more productive.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Story points are a team-local unit, so ten points in one team mean something different in another. Points also drift over time and inflate as soon as velocity becomes a target. Use throughput and cycle time, and compare each team only with its own past.

Read more: [playbook/ways-of-working/planning-and-forecasting.md](../../playbook/ways-of-working/planning-and-forecasting.md)

</details>

### 3. The Scrum Guide time-boxes the Daily Scrum to 15 minutes.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** The 2020 Scrum Guide sets a 15-minute Daily Scrum and Sprints of one month or less. The Daily Scrum is for the Developers to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal. When it turns into a status report to a manager, the team loses the point of it.

Read more: [playbook/ways-of-working/agile-and-scrum.md](../../playbook/ways-of-working/agile-and-scrum.md)

</details>

### 4. A single delivery date is a more useful forecast than a range, because people can plan around it.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** A single date hides the uncertainty, so it becomes a promise that gets broken. Give a range with a confidence level, for example 'between 3 and 6 weeks, 85% likely'. Re-forecast every week as work finishes.

Read more: [playbook/ways-of-working/planning-and-forecasting.md](../../playbook/ways-of-working/planning-and-forecasting.md)

</details>

### 5. A team can forecast a delivery date from its past throughput without estimating any individual task.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** A Monte Carlo forecast replays the team's real history of finished items thousands of times. The result reads as '50% likely within X weeks, 85% within Y'. It needs right-sized items that you count, not hours or points.

Read more: [playbook/ways-of-working/planning-and-forecasting.md](../../playbook/ways-of-working/planning-and-forecasting.md)

</details>

### 6. Most delivery delay comes from engineers working more slowly than they estimated.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Most delay comes from waiting, interruptions and work discovered along the way, not from slow typing. That is why more careful task estimates rarely fix dates. Splitting work small and removing waits does.

Read more: [playbook/ways-of-working/planning-and-forecasting.md](../../playbook/ways-of-working/planning-and-forecasting.md)

</details>

### 7. If work almost always lands inside your 85% forecast range, your ranges are probably too wide.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** An 85% range should be met about 85% of the time. Hitting it nearly every time means the forecast is padded and less useful for planning. Narrow it using your own throughput history.

Read more: [playbook/ways-of-working/planning-and-forecasting.md](../../playbook/ways-of-working/planning-and-forecasting.md)

</details>

### 8. A hardening sprint every few sprints is a healthy way to catch up on quality.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** A regular hardening sprint means work is being called done before it is. Fix the definition of done so tests and quality checks happen with each change. The backlog of defects then stops building up.

Read more: [playbook/ways-of-working/agile-and-scrum.md](../../playbook/ways-of-working/agile-and-scrum.md)

</details>

### 9. The number of features shipped is the best measure of a product team's success.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Counting features rewards a feature factory, whether or not anything improved for users. Agree an outcome metric before work starts and review it after release. Success is a change in user or business behaviour.

Read more: [playbook/ways-of-working/product-partnership.md](../../playbook/ways-of-working/product-partnership.md)

</details>

### 10. Product and engineering should agree how reliability work gets priority before an outage happens, not during one.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Reliability negotiated in the middle of an outage is decided under the worst pressure. An error budget policy agreed in advance, and co-signed by the product owner, settles it ahead of time. When the budget runs out, everyone already knows what happens.

Read more: [playbook/ways-of-working/product-partnership.md](../../playbook/ways-of-working/product-partnership.md)

</details>
